title: Armstrong and classical music; blending melodies in jazz solos
summary: Alcorn says Louis listened to all music and he himself likes symphonies; Louis could mix tunes into Tiger Rag.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Oh yeah. Because they don't run no bands into each other. Yeah. Did he listen to much classical music? Do you know?
I didn't know classical music. No, I said Louis.
Louis? Yeah. Oh, I imagine that he liked it.

Because Louis liked this and any kind of music. And he carried a few records around with him and everything like that. He said I listened to all that. What kind of... Do you know what kind of... Not that he played too much classical music, but he used to listen to all that. I listen to classical music. I don't play classical music.
What kind of classical music do you like particularly?

Well to be honest with you, I said I listen to symphony music. Beethoven? Yeah. Anything like that because there's movements in there. Mm-hmm. We can get something out of it. Sure. You see? And I love to hear that.

Yeah. Just like something we play when you put little raps down like that. Blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. Some of the things I play like that I have a little... Full, full measures of it. You know? And add it into jazz. Put it into a song. That's what it is. The way you feel. Now Louis can sit down and play Tiger Rag and mix it about ten different songs.

You know? When doing the solo. Yeah. Da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, all that kind of different little things. The melodies you hear from other songs. Look what is it? They come out with the songs.
And that's where the jazz thing comes in. That's a, you know, individual thing. Yeah.
